reading.instruction: Read the text and answer the questions in English.
reading.text: When Fatou opened her small fabric shop five years ago, she kept all her accounts in a notebook. Last year, however, she decided to accept mobile money payments. At first, she was worried: many of her older customers did not trust the system, and she was afraid of making mistakes. After a few weeks, things changed. Customers no longer needed to carry cash, and Fatou noticed that people who visited her shop for the first time often came back. Today, about half of her sales are paid by phone. "The technology did not replace my customers' trust," she says. "It simply made it easier for them to come back." Fatou now plans to sell to customers in Nigeria online, but first she wants to improve her English.

reading.instruction: Read the text and answer the questions in English.
reading.text: For many companies, the shift to remote work began as an emergency measure, and few managers expected it to last. Yet several years later, a surprising number of organisations have kept some form of flexible arrangement. Supporters argue that employees save hours of commuting and report higher satisfaction, which in turn reduces staff turnover. Critics, on the other hand, warn that what is gained in comfort may be lost in creativity: spontaneous conversations in corridors, they claim, are where many new ideas are born. The evidence is mixed. Studies suggest that routine tasks are often completed just as efficiently at home, whereas complex projects requiring close collaboration tend to suffer. Perhaps the real lesson is not that one model is better than the other, but that the question "Where should people work?" has been replaced by a more useful one: "What kind of work is being done?"

reading.instruction: Read the text and answer the questions in English.
reading.text: It is often assumed that learning a global language comes at the expense of one's mother tongue, as though the mind had room for only a fixed amount of language. Research on bilingualism suggests otherwise. Far from crowding each other out, languages appear to support one another: children who develop literacy in their first language frequently acquire a second one more easily, not less. The real threat to minority languages is seldom the classroom; it is, more often, the quiet assumption among parents that a language which does not lead to a salary is not worth passing on. Policies that treat linguistic diversity as an obstacle to be managed, rather than a resource to be cultivated, may therefore achieve the opposite of what they intend. None of this denies the very real advantages of English. It simply suggests that the choice so often presented — one language or the other — is, in most cases, a false one.
